summary:
SPHEREx Vision is an interactive astronomy exploration platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx mission data more accessible and understandable. Inspired by SPHEREx's mission to map the entire sky in 102 infrared spectral bands, our platform allows users to explore sky observations, compare observations across different epochs, investigate potential changes, and examine candidate astronomical objects.

By bringing complex astronomical data into an interactive and user-friendly interface, SPHEREx Vision helps users better understand how scientists study the universe through infrared observations and how objects and regions of the sky can change over time.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between large-scale scientific datasets and public understanding, making astronomical exploration more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts while encouraging curiosity and further scientific investigation.
details:
SPHEREx Vision is an interactive astronomy explorer that helps people explore real SPHEREx DR1 infrared survey data. Users can view the sky as a 2D all-sky map or a rotatable 3D globe, browse wavelength bands and false-color spectral views, select sky coordinates, and search for SPHEREx observation coverage. For a region with suitable observations, the app can compare two real observations from different times in the same band, show a diagnostic later-minus-earlier difference, and flag unusual residuals for further inspection.

The project makes a complex astronomy archive more approachable for learning and exploration. Its creative approach combines spectral visualization, sky navigation, archive search, temporal comparison and candidate review in one workflow. Candidate residuals are only leads to investigate—not confirmed objects or discoveries.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Aladin Lite, Three.js and HEALPix tools. The Python backend uses FastAPI and astronomy/scientific packages including Astroquery, Astropy, Reproject, SciPy and Photutils. The project also includes optional MediaPipe hand-tracking controls; camera processing is intended to stay on the user’s device.

We considered data provenance, scientific limitations, clear labeling of false-color and context imagery, archive gaps or failures, and user privacy. The 2MASS and DSS2 backgrounds are navigation context, not SPHEREx data. Comparison results are diagnostic, and candidates require independent validation.
